newsitem.title: UK: BA cargo changes mean new approach, skills.
newsitem.headline: BA cargo changes mean new approach, skills.

text.p: British Airways Plc's plans for reshaping its World Cargo (BAWC) operations at London-Heathrow are part of a worldwide programme, BAWC managing director, Kevin Hatton told Reuters.

Earlier today, BAWC announced it plans to cut 400 jobs over the next two years -- from a workforce of 1,500 -- due to increased automation, although it hopes to avoid any compulsory redundancies by using voluntary severance, redeployment or early retirement.
"We are reconfiguring our business and how we do it. It requires us to do things differently around the world," he added in a telephone interview.
"The way of working will be very different, with very different skills," he added.if

It also means using electronic data interchange (EDI), bar coding to track freight moving through BAWC's network and making use of the latest computer technology ahead of the opening of its new 150 million stg World Cargo Centre in January 1999.

This will be able to handle some 800,000 tonnes of cargo annually, double the present figure. It will include an 87 million stg mechanical handling system and every shipment carried by BA and its corresponding documentation will carry a bar code to speed its movement and reduce errors, the airline said.
In the last financial year, BAWC recorded sales of 563 million stg, compared with BA's overall figure of 7.76 billion stg.
Hatton added that: "It was no surprise he was an admirer of the integrators."
Industry sources said the latter, who include companies such as Federal Express, United Parcel Service of way in providing fast efficient airfreight and express services.

Matching their performance is seen by many industry analysts as one of the top challenges facing the traditional airfreight sector. Express services are forecast to grow at around 18 percent annually for the next 15 years, while airfreight is expected to gain between six percent to 7.5 percent a year.

Hatton said the phased rollout programme for bar coding would start with key areas, the Americas and the Far East. The system will be based on International Air Transport Association (IATA) standards and "a small team of specialists is being assigned" to the project.
He said,"a huge training programme is under way in London with four and a half hour presentations" to groups of 20 staff having started two days ago on February 3.
So far, the initial feedback from these sessions showed," there was a general recognition the business had to change, and there was also a moveaway from "a blame culture," Hatton added.

Staff felt they were, "involved in seeing how the new business will work and it was not just management-speak," and after the meetings, "focus-groups were aiming to see what needed to be done by both sides," he said.
The airline also said a quarter of the 400 jobs involved are now filled by fixed-term staff on contracts ending in 1998 and that this had been made very clear to them when they joined.
